Title: Sustainability, AI, and the new era of corporate reporting
Article:
As universities across the nation prepare to celebrate the success of our new accounting graduates this year, a familiar but pressing question lingers in the minds of many soon-to-be graduates: where do we go from here?
Traditionally, the path to becoming a professional accountant has centred on mastering technical accounting-related competencies such as financial reporting, auditing, taxation, and management accounting. While these competencies remain essential, the accounting profession is presently navigating waves of transformation. With sustainability reporting, and artificial intelligence (AI) gaining global momentum, our graduates are rightfully wondering what this means for their careers. More importantly, what can they do today to remain resilient and competitive in tomorrow's workplace?
The end of standalone reporting
One of the most important shifts in the field is the growing demand for greater credibility and assurance over sustainability information. In the past, organisations could issue sustainability reports with limited external verification. Today, investors, regulators and other stakeholders increasingly expect sustainability-related information to be supported by stronger controls, reliable data and appropriate assurance.
In Malaysia, sustainability reporting is also moving from largely voluntary practice toward formal regulatory requirements. Under the National Sustainability Reporting Framework (NSRF), companies within its scope are progressively required to disclose sustainability-related risks and opportunities using the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, which includes IFRS S1 and IFRS S2. These requirements are intended to improve the consistency, comparability and reliability of sustainability information provided by companies.
Implementation is being phased according to company size and market segment. For companies listed on Bursa Malaysia, large Main Market issuers with a market capitalisation of RM2 billion or more began applying the NSRF requirements for annual reporting periods in 2025, followed by other Main Market issuers from 1 January 2026 and ACE Market issuers from 1 January 2027. The NSRF also extends beyond Bursa-listed companies, with qualifying large non-listed companies with annual revenue of RM2 billion or more required to begin from 1 January 2027.
As sustainability reporting becomes a formal requirement for a wider range of companies, accountants are likely to take on a broader role in managing, interpreting and assuring sustainability-related information. Future professionals may find themselves verifying carbon emissions data, scrutinising climate-related disclosures, assessing sustainability controls, and providing assurance on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) information. Accountants are therefore likely to play a growing role in the verification and assurance of emissions and other sustainability-related information.
Sustainability reporting, however, should not be viewed as a standalone box-ticking exercise relegated to a few pages of an annual report. Instead, organisations are increasingly expected to demonstrate precisely how sustainability considerations drive financial performance, shape business strategy, and contribute to long-term value creation. This fundamentally demands a mindset of 'connected thinking'. The contemporary accountant must possess the acumen to link non-financial issues such as climate risk andsocial equity directly to financial outcomes and organisational risks. The ability to translate these dynamic environmental and social variables into measurable business performance is fast becoming a valuable skill for accounting professionals.
The tech-driven shift to "intelligent" analysis
Simultaneously, technology is expanding the boundaries of the accounting profession. The growing importance of sustainability reporting is closely linked to the rise of digital technologies and artificial intelligence. Sustainability information often draws on large and varied datasets, including emissions, energy use, supply-chain activity, waste, and social indicators, many of which involve estimates and managerial judgement. AI and advanced analytics can help organisations process, compare and interpret this information more efficiently. Yet this introduces new questions for accountants concerning data quality, reliability, bias, traceability, internal controls and assurance, which requires a distinct set of competencies.
By 2026, AI in accounting has evolved far beyond basic automation into predictive risk forecasting and real-time financial visibility. Employers are now increasingly seeking graduates who are not only technically sound but are also highly agile with data analytics tools, digital reporting ecosystems, and AI applications. The future accountant is expected to be a skilled translator, capable of deciphering insights from vast datasets and communicating them effectively to stakeholders.
Furthermore, as climate risk reporting takes centre stage, accountants must step out of their traditional silos. Engaging with disciplines such as environmental science, sustainable engineering, and public policy is now important if they are to meaningfully uphold their role as the primary custodians of integrated business intelligence.
Preparing for a dynamic landscape
A primary developmental focus is sustainability literacy. Today, grasping ESG issues is no longer a peripheral 'good-to-have'; it is a core business imperative. Building a good foundational understanding of ESG issues and global frameworks, such as the ISSB's Sustainability Disclosure Standards, is now a crucial part of an accounting graduate's repertoire. As sustainability ceases to be the exclusive domain of policymakers and environmental scientists, the traditional wall separating the 'accountant' from the 'sustainability professional' is dissolving. The future of corporate reporting demands professionals who can seamlessly integrate these diverse metrics to provide a more holistic picture of organisational health.
Strengthening data and AI literacy will also be increasingly important. The true strength of data analytics lies in its ability to standardise and synthesise massive amounts of messy logistical data, from supply chain traceability metrics to energy consumption records. It is not the main 'hero', yet it will allow accountants to make critical decisions faster. Future accountants will need to do more than operate analytical tools. They must be able to assess data quality, identify unusual patterns, interrogate AI-generated outputs, understand the limitations of analytical models, and communicate the evidence behind their conclusions.
The next step may be to bring these areas even closer together. Future accounting education will need to prepare graduates not only to use AI and analyse sustainability data, but also to question the reliability of that data, understand the controls behind it, exercise professional judgement over AI-generated outputs, and provide assurance over an increasingly broad range of corporate information.
Whether using established tools such as Excel, Power BI, Tableau, or emerging AI applications, the ability to evaluate information critically and exercise sound professional judgement will remain central to accounting work, even as technologies continue tochange. AI-generated analysis can be incomplete, biased or based on unreliable data.
Accountants will therefore need to apply professional scepticism to AI outputs, understand how results were produced, maintain appropriate human oversight, and ensure that decisions remain traceable and accountable. In this respect, AI does not reduce the importance of professional judgement; it makes such judgement even more important.
Perhaps more crucially, embracing lifelong learning is a must. Sustainability standards, reporting frameworks, technology and regulatory requirements will continue to evolve and at times at a rapid pace. The proactive willingness to continuously acquire new knowledge and adapt to changing expectations will be the defining characteristic of a successful future professional.
Accountability: The bedrock of the profession
The contemporary accountant is no longer just steering the financial rudder; they are meant to be visionary leaders with the power to shape environmental and social outcomes. The future of accounting extends beyond the preparation of historical financial reports. As corporate reporting incorporates sustainability information, complex datasets and AI-assisted analysis, accountants will increasingly be called upon to assess the quality, reliability and usefulness of a wider range of information. Their role is therefore not simply to produce more information, but to help ensure that the information used for decision-making can be understood and trusted.
Yet, despite these technical and technological advancements, none can be meaningfully applied without an honest understanding of what it means to be accountable. This principle remains the bedrock of our profession, determining an accountant's true impact on society. While corporate history has offered its share of cautionary tales and examples of ethical lapses, the accountants of tomorrow have now a renewed and expanded opportunity to prove that accountants can be genuine catalysts for positive change.
To the aspiring accountants graduating this year: heartfelt congratulations on completing this major life milestone. As you step into the profession, remember that sustainability and AI are no longer future concepts on a corporate checklist. They are actively rewriting what accountants measure, analyse, question and assure. Used responsibly, these tools provide powerful new ways for the profession to account for good, all while preserving the core pillars of professional judgement, credibility and accountability. AI changes how accountants work; sustainability changes what accountants account for.
But it is your personal accountability that determines your real impact. The ultimate audit you will ever face will not be found within the balances of a corporate ledger, but in the final reckoning of the legacy you leave behind. Your career as an accountant is your opportunity to step up and play a defining role in building a more resilient, accountable, and sustainable Malaysia.
---
The authors are Senior Lecturers within the Faculty of Business and Economics at Universiti Malaya.

Title: Simpan SSPN turns savings into big dreams
Article:
BUKIT MERTAJAM: Beneath BMS 2026's colourful "Under the Sea" theme lies a simple message: start saving today so children can sail towards tomorrow.
For parents attending the Bulan Menabung Simpan SSPN (BMS) 2026 celebration at Mydin Bukit Mertajam here on Saturday, the message came to life through colourful costumes, children's performances, competitions, prizes and interactive activities.
But beneath the excitement was a more serious mission — encouraging Malaysians to prepare financially for their children's education from an early age.
Organised by the National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN), BMS 2026 is being held nationwide from Sept 25 to Nov 1, with celebrations taking place across 14 states at selected locations.
Held with World Savings Day on Oct 31, the campaign carries the theme "Under the Sea" and retains its tagline, "Jom Jadi Superhero Anak Anda!".
The concept likens a child's journey through life and education to an underwater adventure, where every new discovery comes with challenges and uncertainty.
For parents, Simpan SSPN offers one way to prepare for that journey by setting aside money before higher education expenses arise.
PTPTN chairman Datuk Seri Norliza Abdul Rahim said BMS 2026 was a means to strengthen awareness of the importance of education savings.
"BMS 2026 is not merely an annual celebration, but a platform to promote a culture of saving as an early preparation for children's education."
She said Simpan SSPN enabled parents to plan their children's education in a more organised and prudent manner, while supporting PTPTN's efforts to encourage a shift from borrowing towards saving.
The message resonated with visitors at the Penang celebration, including Mohd Hasari Hasan, 46, a Tenaga Nasional Bhd employee and father of four, who won RM15,000 in the WOW! Simpan SSPN Plus 2026 Draw — Cabutan WOW! Simpan SSPN Plus 2026, Series 2 category. Hasari, who started saving through Simpan SSPN in 2021, said he viewed it as a practical way to prepare for his children's education.
[[nid:1547729]]
"Simpan SSPN is not merely a place to save money. It is a platform for parents to make an early commitment towards their children's savings."
His decision to start early has become particularly meaningful as his eldest child, now 18, is studying banking at UiTM Raub, Pahang.
Hasari said the savings had helped with his child's education expenses, allowing him to prepare for university costs without relying entirely on a loan.
He now has Simpan SSPN accounts for all four children, aged between seven and 18.
His advice to other parents was straightforward: do not wait until your children are older.
"I urge parents not to wait until their children are older before opening an account. We can start saving small amounts for our children," he said.
Warehouse officer Chan Tat Beng, 48, said Simpan SSPN had been part of his financial planning for more than a decade.
The father of two children, aged 11 and 14, said he usually made a lump-sum contribution once a year, depending on his financial situation.
[[nid:1547728]]
"For me, it is an opportunity to keep some money safely for our children when they go to university. At least we already have some savings in hand," he said.
Chan was introduced to Simpan SSPN during a visit to Karnival Jom Heboh in Kuala Lumpur more than 10 years ago.
Teacher Norzipah Karim, 48, said she had also opened accounts for her two children years ago to prepare for their education, adding that one had since reached university age.
Customer service executive Siti Nor Aisyah Idrus, 40, from Juru, started saving for her five children in 2018 after learning about Simpan SSPN through a school group.
She makes regular monthly contributions under the Simpan SSPN Plus package and adds more whenever she receives additional income, such as bonuses.
"If I have extra money, I will put more into the children's savings," she said.
Mechanic Azhari Awang, 50, from Kulim, decided to open accounts after visiting the BMS event, saying it gave him the opportunity to act on a plan he had considered for some time.
IT manager Ininl Saminathan, 39, meanwhile, said he also planned to make monthly contributions towards his children's future education.
The parents welcomed the programme, saying it provided greater insight into saving for their children and should continue to be held.
As part of the campaign, PTPTN is promoting various benefits under Simpan SSPN, including income tax relief on savings of up to RM8,000 a year, free takaful protection for depositors, matching grants of up to RM10,000 for eligible families, competitive dividends, government-guaranteed savings and syariah compliance.
The BMS 2026 celebration also featured the presentation of certificates to nine primary schools participating in the Kelab Simpanan Pendidikan module in Penang, as well as prizes for Simpan SSPN campaign winners and the Simpan SSPN Got Talent competition.
PTPTN also presented the Anugerah Permata Inspirasi PTPTN to 11-year-old Nur Amira Safiah Mohamad Zafari, who won a gold medal for public speaking at the International World Innovative Student Exhibition in the United Kingdom.
[[nid:1547727]]
Norliza said the campaign's activities were designed to make financial education more accessible and engaging, particularly for younger Malaysians.
With its colourful "Under the Sea" theme, BMS 2026 seeks to turn the often-serious subject of financial planning into an experience families can enjoy together, while reminding parents that every ringgit saved today can help chart a smoother course towards their children's educational future.

Title: Pro-Imran Khan march starts in Pakistan's northwest
Article:
LAKKI MARWAT, Pakistan: A march protesting the imprisonment of former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan kicked off Sunday in the country's northwest after talks to avoid the demonstration stalled.
Authorities have been preparing for weeks for the possible arrival of demonstrators in Islamabad, with the march planned by supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party originally slated for September 27 and then postponed until Sunday.
In Lakki Marwat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which is ruled by PTI, an AFP journalist saw thousands of people take to the streets.
Many of the demonstrators carried red and green flags of the opposition party, and a huge billboard affixed on the side of a truck read "release Imran Khan" and featured a picture of the beaming former prime minister with his hand held aloft.
Earlier, videos posted on PTI's official social media showed supporters coalescing in different areas in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and setting off in convoys as part of the "long march."
Sohail Afridi, the chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said earlier on X that the demonstration in support of Khan would go ahead.
Discontent over Khan's incarceration has mounted in recent months, particularly over the 73-year-old's medical treatment and access to him by doctors and family.
PTI has also called for the release of Khan's three sisters, whose arrests last month further heightened tensions.
-'Popular support'-
Opposition politician Allama Raja Nasir Abbas said last-minute talks between the government and representatives from PTI were in "deadlock."
Abbas told Geo TV, a popular private news channel, that negotiators had hit an impasse over demands that included access to Khan by his doctor.
Khan, a hugely popular former cricket star, has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges ranging from corruption to treason and inciting violence, following widespread anti-establishment riots in May of that year.
He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralising his popularity.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a geopolitics expert, said the protests were "fundamentally driven by economic factors", with the Iran war impacting fuel prices in Pakistan and food costs rising on the back of the war in Ukraine.
"Day-to-day life has become a real struggle for ordinary Pakistanis in recent years," said Willasey-Wilsey, who is with the UK-based Royal United Services Institute.
"Imran Khan is the focal point for all opposition to the government," he added.
James Dorsey, a fellow at the National University of Singapore, said Khan was "essentially a populist leader" with "a genuine popular movement that had broad popular support."
"That's why I think you've seen the determination by the government to prevent (the protesters) from entering Islamabad," Dorsey said.
Afridi, the chief minister, said the demonstration was to begin in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday and make its way to Khairabad, 80 kilometres (50 miles) west of Islamabad, by Thursday.
- 'Defending Islamabad' -
"The army and police are very capable of defending Islamabad and the government is not under any immediate threat," Willasey-Wilsey said.
"But the problems for Pakistan are piling up," he added.
Dorsey said that with Pakistan's security concerns, particularly following its unresolved February 2026 war with Afghanistan, Islamabad would look to avoid escalation in the face of the protests.
"It's a problem for the government, but I don't think it's an existential threat," he said.
Further phases of the plan would be announced in Khairabad, Afridi said, without specifying when demonstrators could arrive in the Pakistani capital.
Authorities have blocked main access routes to Islamabad with double-stacked shipping containers in preparation for the protest, obstructing traffic and public transit.
The Supreme Court ruled in August that Khan should be moved to a civilian hospital for treatment, but authorities instead returned him to prison after a short stay at a government-run hospital.

Title: Amanah, DAP differ over PH cooperation with Bersatu in Melaka
Article:
MELAKA:  Parti Amanah Negara is at odds with DAP over possible political cooperation between Pakatan Harapan and other political coalitions or parties for the Melaka election.
Amanah secretary-general Muhammad Faiz Fadzil said the party was more inclined to work with political partners it considered sincere rather than go it alone.
He said sincerity among coalition partners was important as it formed the basis for a stable government.
"Amanah's position is to seek sincere partners to govern Melaka. Sincerity will create stability in the government.
"Without sincerity, the government will not be stable, as seen in Negri Sembilan when the 'blue wave' turned into chaos," he said after attending the AgroMadani Sales Programme and an engagement session with fishermen at the Tanjung Nibong Fishermen's Complex in Telok Mas here yesterday.
Also present were Agriculture and Food Security Minister's political secretary Yuhaizad Abdullah and Malaysian Fisheries Development Authority state director Darleena Baharuddin.
Faiz was commenting on a statement by Melaka DAP chairman Khoo Poay Tiong, who was reported to have said that Melaka PH would contest the state election on its own and would not cooperate with Bersatu or parties outside the coalition.
Khoo, who is also Melaka PH deputy chairman, was quoted as saying that the coalition would contest all 28 seats in the
state election.
However, Melaka PH chairman Adly Zahari said on Oct 1 that room for negotiations with various parties remained open, including the possibility of forming a PH Plus cooperation.
Adly had said that the final decision would be made by the PH Presidential Council before nomination day.
Faiz said  although there were differing views among PH component parties, Amanah had its own position.
"There are views within PH against cooperating with parties outside the coalition.
"We take those views into consideration, but from Amanah's perspective, I believe it is better to unite with allies to form a stable government in Melaka.
"The identity of potential partners cannot be revealed yet, but the door for negotiations with various parties remains open," he said.
He added that the decision on which allies would work with Amanah in the Melaka election would be announced soon.

Title: J-KOM boosting communication efforts on social media
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
SEBERANG PRAI: The Community Communications Department (J-KOM) is placing greater emphasis on social media, giving it 70 per cent of its communication efforts to ensure government messages and achievements reach the people.
Its director-general, Mohd Hisyamuddin Ghazali, said the shift was necessary as social media had become one of the main channels through which people obtain information.
The remaining 30 per cent would focus on outreach programmes and field activities, such as the Madani Kita Programme (PMK), which allows the government to engage directly with the public.
"Without a strong presence on social media, government messages will not reach the grassroots.
"PMK complements this by explaining government policies and achievements directly to the people, especially when negative messages circulating on social media can overshadow these achievements," he said after a PMK event here yesterday.
The event, launched by Penang Housing and Environment Committee chairman and Prai assemblyman Datuk Seri S. Sundarajoo, drew nearly 2,000 visitors.
On preparations for the Melaka election, Hisyamuddin said J-KOM would intensify efforts to provide fact-based information to help voters make informed choices.
"For the Melaka election, we will do our best to convey positive messages to the people.
"The information we provide is based on facts about the achievements of Malaysia Madani under the leadership of Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, so that the people can make the best choice."
Hisyamuddin said PMK served as a platform for J-KOM to engage with communities and obtain feedback on government policies and performance.
Participants are required to complete survey forms, allowing J-KOM to gauge public views and identify areas for improvement.
The PMK event yesterday brought together 37 departments and agencies, providing access to information on public services, assistance, facilities and initiatives.

Title: Malaysia, Thailand boost flood aid coordination
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
SONGKHLA: The Consulate-General of Malaysia in Songkhla and Thai authorities have agreed to establish a mechanism to improve the distribution of flood aid.
Malaysia's Consul-General in Songkhla Ahmad Fahmi Ahmad Sarkawi said this was part of preparations to deal with the possibility of major floods such as those that hit Hat Yai last November.
He said warehouses that could be used to store supplies from Malaysia had been identified.
"When supplies from Malaysia arrive, we will immediately send them to the warehouses.
"We have also agreed that Thai authorities will distribute the supplies to those in need," Fahmi said during a visit by a Perlis Journalists Association delegation to his office here recently.
He said if Thai authorities did not have enough manpower, non-governmental organisations from Malaysia could help.
"This is based on lessons learnt from last year's major floods, when relief supplies from Malaysia piled up in Hat Yai because it was unclear who would distribute or store them."
Fahmi said the consulate was coordinating with agencies in Malaysia to ensure aid could be channelled more easily from Thailand should floods occur in Malaysia's northern states.
On last year's major floods in southern Thailand, he said about 7,000 Malaysians were rescued.
He advised Malaysians planning to travel to southern Thailand between this month and January to monitor weather developments.
He said the consulate had learnt from last year's major floods and would issue weather warnings from the Thai authorities more frequently through its website and social media platforms

Title: Middle East carriers fight back
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia and other Asia-Pacific aviation markets could face stronger competition for international passengers as Middle Eastern airlines seek to win back traffic lost to Asian carriers following disruptions earlier this year.
Association of Asia Pacific Airlines (AAPA) director-general Wong Hong told Business Times: "You may get some shift, but Middle Eastern carriers are not going to give up without a fight.
"They will try to win customers back and take back the business they lost during the last four months."
"Whether it comes back to the same level is the question."
Since tensions began in the Middle East, several Asia-Pacific airlines have seen an increase in transit traffic as passengers opted for alternative routes through Asian hubs.
For example, Cathay Pacific said in March that Middle East disruptions had shifted passenger demand towards other aviation hubs, with more passengers transiting through Hong Kong.
The airline has added flights and increased capacity to Europe as travellers seek alternative routes.
On airfares, Hong said it was difficult to predict whether fares would rise or fall, as prices depend on market conditions and how aggressively airlines compete for passengers.
"Airfares are determined by supply and demand. If an airline puts out a particular airfare and the bookings do not come, what do you think it is going to do?
"Airlines need to be realistic. It comes down to what the market can bear and customers' willingness to pay."
Hong said airlines are also monitoring fuel prices as the industry approaches the end of the year.
He said regional airlines are hoping for a return to normal operations, with fuel prices stabilising at more manageable levels.
"If demand continues to hold up despite the inflationary risks, then I think that going into 2027, we will return to business as usual."
